text: The personality test said I score low on extraversion and high on conscientiousness, which honestly did not surprise me at all. I have always been the person who prepares everything in advance and then says very little in the actual meeting. That is simply how I am.

To be honest I was quite hesitant when I read that half of this course would be together with students in Zurich. I do not mind group work as such, but doing it in English with people I have never met feels like a lot to ask in week one. Right now I am mostly nervous about it.

The hallmarks of cancer were mostly familiar from my bachelor, although I had never looked at deregulated cellular energetics in any detail. That lecture was the one I found most interesting this week.

We had our first real meeting with the Zurich group. It was awkward for the first ten minutes and then it was fine. They were friendly and one of them had already set up a shared document, which helped more than I expected.

I realised during that meeting that I had assumed everybody would just start talking the way we do in Utrecht, where interrupting is more or less how you show interest. The Zurich students waited for each other to finish. I felt quite rude for a moment and then adjusted.

I actually look forward to the Thursday calls now, which I would not have predicted in week one. It has become the part of the week where I hear how a completely different group approached the same paper.
I have started speaking more slowly and I avoid the Dutch expressions that do not translate. It makes the discussion easier for everyone, and I think my English has improved as a side effect.
The proteomics block was hard.
I am totally motivated to do something international again after this. I have already looked into whether there is an exchange option in my master. Six months ago I would have said absolutely not.

I am still an introvert and I still need a day to recover after a long online session, and that has not changed at all. What did change is that I no longer assume being quiet means I contributed less than the others.

I am really excited about this course, mostly because of the international part. I am Italian and I have always found it easy to talk to people from anywhere, so I suspect this will be the easiest element of the whole semester for me.

My own culture is quite expressive and we interrupt each other constantly, which people from elsewhere sometimes read as arguing. It is not arguing. Knowing that about myself at least lets me explain it when somebody looks alarmed.
I had never seen a Circos plot before this week and I remain unconvinced that they are the clearest way to present structural variants.

Finding a time slot that worked for both sites took us four days of messages for a thirty minute meeting. I understand there is only one hour of difference between us, but somehow it was still a nightmare.
There are only three students left in Zurich, which makes the whole COIL idea feel rather thin. In our group of six we are five from Utrecht and one from Zurich, so in practice it is us plus a guest.

I have stopped thinking of the international element as a real part of the course. We do the joint session because it is on the schedule, and afterwards everyone goes back to working with whoever is sitting next to them.
The paper discussions themselves are good. Reading a methods section properly and then arguing about whether the controls were adequate is the most useful thing I have done this semester.
If I am honest I would not choose the COIL version of this course again. Not because international collaboration is a bad idea, but because doing it badly is worse than not doing it at all.

I also have to admit that I am impatient with people who do not answer messages within a day, and that is probably as much a cultural thing on my side as on theirs. I am not certain I gave them a fair chance.

I grew up in Biel where you switch between German and French on the same street, so a course taught in English with students from another country does not feel unusual to me. It is more or less how I did my schooling.
I am curious about how the Utrecht students actually work. I have heard their programme is far more group based than ours and I would like to see for myself whether that is true.
Week one was very heavy on definitions. I would have preferred to start from a case and work backwards to the mechanisms.
The joint session worked well. We split the paper into four parts and each pair presented one section. Nobody was left with nothing to do, which in my experience is rare in group work.
I notice that I automatically become considerably more formal in English than I ever am in German. That is not something I decide to do, it is simply what happens to me in a second language.

I learned that in the Netherlands it is quite normal to disagree with a supervisor directly, in front of the whole group. In Switzerland that conversation would happen afterwards and in private. Seeing the difference was genuinely useful to me.
Was fine this week.
I would do this course again and I would tell other students to take it. The international part is the reason it is worth the extra work it costs.

I am a fairly reserved person and I did not turn into the most talkative member of the group. But I was never uncomfortable either, and I think that is partly because I am used to not working in my first language.
I am not sure yet what to think about the international part of this course. Will we genuinely work together, or will it just be two groups presenting at each other once a week?
In my family everything is decided together and loudly. I bring that into group work, for better and for worse, and people who prefer quiet orderly meetings tend to find me a lot.

The Zurich students are well prepared, which is good, but they also settled the structure of the whole report before asking us. I was annoyed for a day, and then I realised we had done exactly the same thing to them with the slides.
Single cell RNA sequencing was the highlight of the block for me. I had no idea you could resolve the tumour microenvironment at that level of detail.
I was hesitant at first, I admit that openly. Now I would say the international sessions are the only reason I still remember anything at all from week four.
Online only is the problem here. Not the countries, the screen. If we had met once in person at the start, everything after that would have been easy.
Good course. Too long.
I know now that I need to see a person's face before I really trust their work. That is a fact about me rather than anything to do with Zurich.

I am looking forward to this course more than any other this semester, mainly because of the collaboration with Zurich. My mother is from Shanghai and my father is Dutch, and I grew up switching between a household where you never contradict an elder and a school where you are more or less graded on contradicting your teacher. I have spent my whole life translating between those two, so an international project feels less like a challenge and more like a normal Tuesday.
The hallmarks framework is elegant, but I do wonder how much of it survives contact with an actual clinical tumour sample.

Something I noticed this week. When the Zurich group went quiet after I made a suggestion, my very first thought was that they disagreed with me. In my mother's family, silence after a proposal means it is being taken seriously. I had to actively stop myself from over-explaining the whole thing.
The workload distribution was not fair in this block. Two of us did the entire analysis while four people did the formatting, and I was one of the two. Nobody said anything about it.

The best moment so far was when the Zurich student and I discovered we had been given contradictory instructions by our two supervisors, and simply decided between ourselves which one to follow. That felt like actual collaboration rather than a scheduled activity.
I am someone who apologises before asking a question. I have been told more than once that it makes me sound unsure of my own data. It comes from home and I do not think it is going to go away.

There was a real disagreement in our group in week nine that we never resolved. One person stopped replying entirely and we finished the report without them. I do not think anybody handled it well, myself included.

Looking back I was totally motivated by the end, which surprises me, because I started this course assuming the international element would be decoration. What changed my mind was not a lecture but a forty minute argument about normalisation methods.
I understand now that I read directness as rudeness considerably faster than my Dutch classmates do, and that this is something I brought with me rather than something they did to me.
